findings.situation: A filer who lived all of 2025 in Albany or Buffalo (outside New York City) truthfully answers No to the city question, so the State question is never asked and the line is set to false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30, Resident: "You are a New York State resident for income tax purposes if: • You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more in New York State ... • Your domicile is New York State."
findings.why: The line's own description says it is the State question asked only after a No to the city question. The gate does the opposite: it asks it only after a Yes. Inside that branch, a city resident gets "No", so the State residency answer can never reach the filers it is meant for.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the filer lived in New York City all year but the spouse did not. The filer answers Yes for themselves, and the residency status that matters for the spouse is never determined.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31, New York City and Yonkers: "see the definitions of a New York State resident, nonresident, and part-year resident above, and substitute New York City or Yonkers in place of New York State."
findings.why: The gate question asks only about "you". The gated helper asks about "you (and your spouse, on a joint return)", so the gate does not cover the spouse.

findings.situation: A person domiciled outside New York City keeps a permanent place of abode in the city for substantially all of the year and spends 184 or more days there. That person is a city resident under the cited test, but may truthfully say they did not 'live in' the city all year.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30: "You maintain a permanent place of abode in New York State for substantially all of the tax year and spend 184 days or more ... whether or not you were domiciled in New York State"; p. 31: "substitute New York City ... in place of New York State"
findings.why: The cited text defines residence by domicile, or by a permanent place of abode plus 184 days. The gate instead asks whether the filer 'lived in' the city all year, which is a different condition.

findings.situation: A New York City domiciliary spent most of 2025 on a temporary work assignment elsewhere and does not count it as 'time away' while their 'home stayed in the city'. Such a filer could reasonably answer No.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 30, Domicile: "If you move to a new location but intend to stay there only for a limited amount of time (no matter how long), your domicile does not change."
findings.why: 'Did you live in New York City' reads as physical presence. The help text's reference to time away does not clearly tell a filer on a long-term relocation that domicile governs.

findings.why: The gate's stated wording covers the spouse, but the f2441 helper questions it is actually computed from say only "you." A filer who is the student or disabled spouse could truthfully answer no, which zeroes line 64 when the federal credit, and so the New York credit, would apply.

findings.situation: On a joint return, the spouse rather than the filer paid the care expenses. The helper "Did you pay for the care..." could be read as asking only about the filer's own payments.

findings.situation: A farmer files federal Schedule F (no Schedule C, no rental or royalty property) and took bonus depreciation on farm machinery placed in service after June 1, 2003 that is still in use in 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "If you claimed a depreciation deduction for such property; and no exception for resurgence zone or New York liberty zone property applies, then complete Part 1 of Form IT-398"
findings.why: S-213 applies to any depreciation deduction for IRC § 168(k) property, including farm property on Schedule F. The computed condition checks only for a Schedule C or for rental or royalty property, so it is false and the question is never asked.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C and no rental property is a partner, S corporation shareholder, or beneficiary whose entity claimed IRC § 168(k) depreciation and reports a New York depreciation amount to the filer.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "Partners, shareholders, and beneficiaries: Do not complete Form IT-398 to determine the amount to enter. Enter the amount provided to you by the entity of which you are a partner, shareholder, or beneficiary"
findings.why: S-213 gives a pass-through owner an amount even without a Schedule C or rental property. The computed condition is false for such a filer, so the gated question is not reached unless another line handles the pass-through amount.

findings.situation: A filer with no Schedule C and no rental property claims depreciation, including bonus depreciation, on a vehicle or equipment on federal Form 2106 (for example, a reservist, performing artist, or fee-basis government official).
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 21, S-213: "If you claimed a depreciation deduction for such property"
findings.why: S-213 does not limit the rule to Schedule C or rental property. Bonus depreciation on employee business property claimed on Form 2106 falls under S-213, but the computed condition is false for this filer.

findings.situation: A filer or spouse is a partner in a partnership, LLC or LLP and has more than $50,000 of net earnings from self-employment allocated to Zone 1, but has no Schedule C, so the computed count is 0.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "For purposes of the MCTMT, self-employed individuals include: • Sole proprietors • Partners in partnerships • Members of limited liability companies (LLCs) that are treated as partnerships • Partners of limited liability partnerships (LLPs)"
findings.why: The condition counts only Schedule C filers. Partnership self-employment earnings reported on a K-1 make the filer subject to MCTMT, yet the condition stays false and the question is never asked.

findings.situation: A filer has a single Schedule C with net profit of $50,000 or less, plus partnership or farm (Schedule F) self-employment earnings, and the combined total allocated to one zone exceeds $50,000.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "You must calculate your MCTMT net earnings base separately for each source of self-employment income ... If you have more than one source, combine all the individual amounts on line 54a ... or line 54b"
findings.why: The $50,000 test applies to net earnings from self-employment from all sources combined. A count limited to Schedule C, with either more than one Schedule C or a single profit over $50,000, misses a person whose earnings exceed the threshold only through non-Schedule C sources.

findings.situation: A filer's Schedule C profit exceeds $50,000, but the business operates entirely outside the MCTD, or the net earnings allocated to each zone (after the 92.35% self-employment adjustment) are $50,000 or less.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 15: "If an individual's net earnings from self-employment allocated to either zone exceed $50,000 for the tax year, then you are subject to the MCTMT."
findings.why: The condition ignores zone allocation and uses net profit rather than net earnings from self-employment, so it holds in some cases where no MCTMT applies. This costs the filer only an extra question.

findings.situation: A full-year New York State resident who moved into New York State outside New York City on January 1, 2025 and has a 2025 bonus paid in 2026.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "Full-year New York State residents You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 and • you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or • you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026."
findings.why: The gate is false because there was no move into New York City, but the cited text subjects this full-year New York State resident with accrued income to special accruals.

findings.situation: A New York City part-year resident for 2025 who moved into New York City mid-year and has accrued income.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "Full-year and part-year New York City residents You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 ... and you were a: ... • New York City part-year resident for tax year 2025."
findings.why: The gate only catches a move into New York City at the start of 2025 or out at the start of 2026, so a mid-year move makes it false even though the text applies special accruals to any New York City part-year resident with accrued income.

findings.situation: The cited text conditions special accruals on accrued income plus specified New York State or New York City residency status at the year boundaries, not merely on moving into or out of New York City at the start of a year.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025 and • you were a nonresident of New York State on December 31, 2024; or • you will be a New York State nonresident on January 1, 2026."
findings.why: The gate substitutes a New York City move event for the text’s accrued-income and New York State/New York City residency-status conditions, and it omits New York State residents outside New York City.

findings.situation: A filer who moved into New York City on January 1, 2025 but has no accrued income at all.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 31: "You are subject to the special accrual rules only if you have accrued income for 2025..."
findings.why: The gate holds on the move alone, so the tool asks the gated question even though the text gives no special-accrual amount without accrued income.

findings.situation: A filer who is only the designated beneficiary of a New York 529 account, not its owner, receives a 2025 withdrawal partly included in federal AGI.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "Beneficiary During 2025, did you, as a beneficiary, receive a withdrawal from one or more tuition savings accounts established under New York's 529 college savings program? ... If Yes, and you included part of the withdrawal in your federal adjusted gross income ... then enter that amount on line 30."
findings.why: The computed condition asks whether the filer 'Owned an account in New York's 529 college savings program', so a non-owner beneficiary truthfully answers no and line 30 is zero. The gated question 'did you ... put money into that New York 529 account, or take any out?' also does not clearly reach a beneficiary who received a withdrawal from someone else's account.

findings.situation: An account owner contributed to a New York 529 account in 2025 but took no distribution, so nothing about the account appears on the federal return.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "as an account owner, made contributions, enter the amount up to $5,000 ($10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return) on line 1 of the Line 30 worksheet."
findings.why: The outer helper 'A 529 plan, Coverdell or ABLE account on the return' can truthfully be answered no when there is no Form 1099-Q and no federal entry, because 529 contributions are not reported federally. The computed condition then becomes 'No' and the contribution subtraction is dropped.

findings.situation: On a joint return, only the spouse owns the New York 529 account, and it had contributions or a nonqualified withdrawal in 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 8, A-103: "If you are filing a joint return, include the applicable amounts from all existing accounts owned by you and your spouse"; ny_it201i p. 10: "$10,000 for married taxpayers filing a joint return"
findings.why: The gating helper 'Owned an account in New York's 529 college savings program at any time in 2025' does not mention the spouse. A filer can answer no about their own ownership, which skips both gated questions even though those questions themselves cover the spouse.

findings.situation: A filer owned a New York 529 account in 2025 but made no contributions or withdrawals.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 10, Line 30: "During 2025, did you, as an account owner, make contributions to or a withdrawal from ... If No, go to line 31."
findings.why: Ownership at any time in 2025 is broader than the cited contribution-or-withdrawal condition. This only costs extra questions.

findings.situation: A recipient born January through June 1966 turns 59½ during 2025 and qualifies for the exclusion on amounts received after that date, but the computed condition 'born in 1965 or earlier' is false.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: "If you became 59½ during 2025, enter only the amount you received after you became 59½, but not more than $20,000."
findings.why: Anyone born on or before June 30, 1966 reaches 59½ during 2025, so the birth-year cutoff of 1965 drops these filers. The gate then never asks the question, and the exclusion becomes zero.

findings.situation: A recipient under 59½ received pension or IRA income as the beneficiary of a decedent, so the condition is false and the question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: "If you received pension and annuity income ... as a beneficiary, see Married taxpayers or Beneficiaries below."
findings.why: A beneficiary can qualify through the decedent regardless of the beneficiary's own age. The gated question asks about this case, but the age-based gate prevents it from ever being asked.

findings.situation: When the condition holds, the gated line always resolves to 'No'. The gated question appears only in the branch where the condition is false, and that branch is unreachable behind this gate, so the question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: "Did you enter an amount of pension income or annuity income, or both ... that was not from a New York State or local government pension plan or federal government pension plan?"
findings.why: The line is designed for younger recipients, such as those turning 59½ in 2025 or beneficiaries. This gate requires the opposite condition, so every situation where the line matters is excluded.

findings.situation: The gate tests birth in 1965 or earlier, while the cited text tests reaching 59½ before January 1, 2025, with partial relief for those reaching 59½ during 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 29: "If Yes, and you were 59½ before January 1, 2025 ..."; "If you became 59½ during 2025 ..."
findings.why: Being born in 1965 is not the same as being 59½ before 2025: those born July through December 1965 reach 59½ in 2025. The text's 2025 window also extends to births through June 30, 1966. The helper's label ('59½ or older at some time in 2025') does not match its computation either.

findings.situation: A filer receives or pays alimony in 2025 under two instruments: one entered into before 2019 and one executed after 2018.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 10, A-119: "If you received any applicable alimony or separate maintenance payments during the tax year, then enter the amount received. An applicable alimony or separate maintenance payment is a payment made under an alimony or separation instrument ... that was executed after December 31, 2018."; i1040gi p. 89, Line 2a: "If you are including alimony payments from more than one divorce or separation agreement in your income, enter the total"
findings.why: The pre-2019 agreement makes the filer truthfully answer yes to the s1 question, so the computed condition is true. The NY question is asked only when it is false, so the post-2018 applicable alimony is dropped from A-119/S-136.

findings.situation: A filer must include or may deduct a recapture of alimony under an old agreement, and also pays or receives alimony in 2025 under an instrument executed after 2018.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 18, S-136: "If you made any applicable alimony or separate maintenance payments during the tax year, then enter the amount paid."
findings.why: The recapture alone makes the s1 condition true, so the question about applicable post-2018 alimony is never asked.

findings.situation: A pre-2019 divorce instrument was modified after 2018 to expressly provide that the Tax Law § 612(w) modifications apply, and payments under it were made in 2025.
findings.irs_text: ny_it225i p. 10, A-119: "This also applies to any divorce or separation instrument executed on or before December 31, 2018, and modified after December 31, 2018, if the modification to the instrument expressly provides that the addition and subtraction modifications contained in Tax Law § 612(w) apply."; s1 question: "under a divorce or separation agreement entered into on or before December 31, 2018"
findings.why: The filer truthfully answers yes to the s1 question, because the agreement was entered into before 2019 and the question does not mention modification. The condition is then true, and the NY applicable-alimony question is skipped even though these payments are applicable alimony for New York.

findings.situation: A filer who answered no to paying or receiving alimony since 2023 is then asked about "that alimony".

findings.why: "That alimony" has no clear referent. The question never states that it means payments under an instrument executed after 2018, or under a pre-2019 instrument modified to adopt § 612(w), so a filer could read it either way.

findings.situation: A filer withdrew money from the New York 529 account and spent it on college costs that are not qualified higher education expenses, such as travel, or spent it at a school that is not an eligible educational institution, such as some foreign schools. The filer would truthfully answer No because the money was used 'for college', so the tool enters $0 on line 22.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "A withdrawal from a New York 529 college savings program is considered nonqualified unless it is used: • to pay the qualified higher education expenses of the designated beneficiary at an eligible educational institution as defined in Education Law § 695-b(5)"
findings.why: The New York text excuses only qualified higher education expenses paid to an eligible educational institution. The question excuses anything spent 'for college', which is broader. Withdrawals for non-qualified college costs or ineligible schools need the Line 22 worksheet but would get a No answer.

findings.situation: Before July 4, 2025, a filer paid tuition from the New York 529 account to a vocational or trade school that is an eligible educational institution. Following the help text, the filer would answer Yes, even though the withdrawal is qualified and the tool's $0 is correct.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "to pay the qualified higher education expenses of the designated beneficiary at an eligible educational institution as defined in Education Law § 695-b(5)"; "to pay the qualified postsecondary credentialing expenses ... on or after July 4, 2025"
findings.why: The help says 'Career training is No only if paid from July 4, 2025', so a filer who thinks of trade-school tuition as career training rather than 'college' would answer Yes. In fact, tuition at an eligible postsecondary institution is a qualified higher education expense on any date.

findings.situation: A filer, or a filer and spouse on a joint return, owns more than one New York 529 account, and the nonqualified withdrawal came from an account other than the one the filer has in mind.
findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 8, Line 22: "Did you make a nonqualified withdrawal during 2025 from an account established under New York’s 529 college savings program?"; worksheet line 1 "from your accounts"

findings.irs_text: ny_it201i p. 9, Line 28: "Dividends you received from a regulated investment company (mutual fund) that invests in obligations of the U.S. government and meet the 50% asset requirement each quarter qualify for this subtraction. The portion of the qualifying dividends that may be subtracted is based upon the portion of the taxable income received by the mutual fund that is derived from federal obligations."
findings.why: The question asks whether any interest or dividends came from "a fund that holds them," without the 50% asset test or the federal-obligation-portion limit. A filer with a nonqualifying or partly qualifying fund must answer YES and the tool refuses line 28, even though the correct line 28 amount is zero or only a portion.

question:
a box on a tick-box screen. The filer ticks it for YES, and leaves it unticked or chooses "None of these" for NO.
  Screen heading: Did any of your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) interest or dividends come from these?
  Label beside the box: U.S. government bonds, notes or bills, or a fund holding them
  Question shown under the box's "What this asks": Was any of your (or, on a joint return, your spouse's) interest or dividends from U.S. government obligations, such as Treasury bills, notes or bonds, savings bonds, bonds of a U.S. government agency, or a fund that holds them?
